Finally Jesus, circumcising the people with a second circumcision, speaks thus: "Today I have taken away from you the reproach of Egypt." So long as we sin, so long as the vices of the passions reign in us, even though, having abandoned the images, we seem to have departed from Egypt, yet the "reproach of Egypt" has not been taken away from us. If therefore you receive this second circumcision of the vices and cut away from yourself every vice of anger, pride, envy, lust, avarice, iniquity and the rest of the like, then the "reproaches of Egypt" will be wiped away from you, and, carried over into the land of promise, you will receive the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, through the true Jesus, Christ our Lord and Savior, "to whom is glory unto the ages of ages. Amen."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Those who were disobedient to the commands of the Lord are called uncircumcised. From this it is understood that those are named uncircumcised who do not obey the commandments of God. But nevertheless both the circumcised and the uncircumcised — because God loves every soul — he does not utterly abandon. For he sent Jesus, who would circumcise all at once, both the worthy and the unworthy — not Jesus the son of Nave, for that man did not circumcise the people with a true and perfect circumcision — but Jesus our Lord and Savior. For it is he who truly cuts away from us the pollution of the flesh and purges from our heart and soul the defilements of sins. Listen, then, to what Scripture says in those things which were prefigured through the son of Nave. "But the children of Israel, having been circumcised," it says, "rested, sitting in the same place in the camp, until they were healed. And then the Lord said to Jesus: this day I have taken away the reproach of Egypt from you." For it is not enough for us to be "circumcised," but also after circumcision to be "healed," that is, until the very wound of circumcision closes over with a scar. When, then, is the scar closed over the wound of our circumcision? I judge it thus, that to be circumcised through our Jesus is to lack vices, to lay aside evil habits and the worst practices, to cut away foul and disordered manners and whatever shrinks back from the rule of honor and piety. But when we do this in the beginnings, we are constrained by the very difficulty, so to speak, of the newness, and as though with a certain labor and grief of soul we change the faults of our old habit by a new practice. And therefore there is, as I said, a certain difficulty in the beginnings, and only with hardship and pain are we able to amputate the first things and take up the second. This, then, seems to me to be the time in which, as though in the pain of our circumcision, we are said "to remain, until," the scar having closed, "we are healed." And we close the scar when we now fulfill the new practices without difficulty, and what before seemed difficult, as being unaccustomed, turns into a habit for us. And then indeed we are said truly to be "healed," when, lacking vices, by a new practice we turn virtue into nature.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Let us see, however, what this very thing is which is said: "today I have taken away the reproach from the children of Israel." All men, even if they come from the law, even if they have been instructed through Moses, nevertheless have "the reproach of Egypt" in themselves, the "reproach" of sins. Who will be like Paul even according to the observance of the law? Hear then him himself saying: "according to the righteousness which is in the law, having conducted myself without blame." Yet he himself declares and says: "for we too were once foolish, unbelieving, going astray, serving desires and various pleasures, in malice and envy, hateful, hating one another." Do these things not seem to you to be "reproaches," and "reproaches of Egypt"? But from the time that Christ came and gave us the second circumcision "through the washing of regeneration" and cleansed our souls, we cast off all these things and in their place took up the pledge of a good conscience toward God. Then through the second circumcision the "reproaches of Egypt" were taken away from us and the vices of sins were cleansed. Let no one, therefore, if he has been wholly converted, if he has repented from the heart, if he has faithfully departed from the streams of the Jordan, if he has been cleansed by the second circumcision through the gospel, fear the "reproaches" of past transgressions. You hear that "today I have taken away from you the reproach of Egypt." This the Lord signifies also in the Gospels, when he says: "your sins are forgiven you," "but now sin no more, lest something worse befall you." For if after the remission of sins you sin no more, truly "the reproach of Egypt has been taken away from you." But if you sin again, again the old reproaches are rolled back upon you, all the more so as it is a much greater crime "to trample the Son of God underfoot and to count the blood of the covenant a polluted thing" than to neglect the law of Moses. For much greater is the reproach of him who fornicates after the gospel than of him who, being placed under the law, does so, because this one, taking away "the members of Christ, makes them members of a harlot." You see, then, how much graver and more heaped-up are the reproaches that are rolled back upon you, if you have been negligent. Indeed, now no one accuses you as guilty of debauchery, but condemns you for the crime of sacrilege, because it is said to you: "know you not that your bodies are the temple of God?"; "but if any man violate the temple of God, God shall destroy him." Even if you were formerly ignorant of these things, yet now, from the time that these words are spoken in your ears and a doctrine of this kind is poured into your heart, know that, having heard these things, you have now been made "the temple of God" and "a member of Christ." See how much you have advanced from an earthly little man: you have without doubt progressed into "the temple of God," in which God ought to dwell, and you who were flesh and blood have advanced so as to be "a member of Christ." But just as this advance is great, so also the departure is terrible and the fall irremediable. For now it is not permitted to you to use "the temple of God" except in holiness, nor to recall "the members of Christ" to an unworthy business. And therefore, if ever the enticement of some evil concupiscence assails you, mindful of these things which you now hear, go to meet that enemy who "proceeds from" your very self, that is, "from your heart," and resist him in such words as these; say: "I am not my own, for I have been bought with a price," "the blood of Christ," and I have been made "a member" of him—it is not permitted to me "to take a member of Christ and make it a member of a harlot." Say to him that I have been made "the temple of God"—it is not permitted to me to bring anything unclean in there, nor is it lawful for me to violate "the temple of God." But add this too, that "he who fornicates sins against his own body," not only against this body which has been made "the temple of God," but also against that which is spoken of, that the whole "church is the body of Christ," and he seems to offend against the whole church who defiles his own body, because through one member the stain is diffused into the whole body. There is also that "reproach of Egypt" which, if you have been negligent, is suggested even after the crossing of the Jordan and after the second circumcision of baptism by the branding of old habit: to observe auguries, to inquire into the courses of the stars and to search out the outcomes of future events from these, to keep omens, and to become entangled in the other superstitions of this kind. For Egypt is the mother of idolatry, from which it is certain that "reproaches" of this kind sprout up; and if, when the Jordan has already been crossed, you take these up and again bind yourself in these snares, you without doubt drag "the reproaches of Egypt" along with you. But if ever such curiosity accosts you and an enemy of this kind bursts forth "from" your "heart," say to him that I follow Jesus as my leader, in whose power are the things that are to come. What need have I to know the things that are to come, since the things which he wills are the things that shall be? Therefore, in order that in us the second circumcision may be truly completed, through which we may lay aside the old "reproaches of Egypt," we ought to be utterly separated from all these things, so that, purified in body and heart, we may also "lift up pure hands" to God, and with a pure mouth also and cleansed lips and a sincere mind, we may by prayer and deeds glorify God in Christ Jesus our Lord, "whose is the power and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: What does it profit, if we fast for our sins and again commit sins? What does it profit to have washed and again to wallow in the mire? Have you fasted for some time? It is as though in the meantime you had departed from Egypt. You have crossed the Red Sea, you have followed Moses, observing that is to say the precepts and commandments of the law; but now Jesus has received you from Moses, who also "circumcises you a second time," in the place which is called "the hill of foreskins." You must therefore be circumcised not only of the worship of idols, which you cast away in the beginning, but again avarice too must be circumcised from you, which is the subtler worship of idols. Finally Jesus, circumcising the people with a second circumcision, speaks thus: "Today I have taken away from you the reproach of Egypt." So long as we sin, so long as the vices of the passions reign in us, even though, having abandoned the images, we seem to have departed from Egypt, yet the "reproach of Egypt" has not been taken away from us. If therefore you receive this second circumcision of the vices and cut away from yourself every vice of anger, pride, envy, lust, avarice, iniquity and the rest of the like, then the "reproaches of Egypt" will be wiped away from you, and, carried over into the land of promise, you will receive the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom, through the true Jesus, Christ our Lord and Savior, "to whom is glory unto the ages of ages. Amen."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And so at last the divine word rightly says to us those things which follow: "this day I have taken away the reproach of Egypt from you," because, after "the reproach of Egypt was taken away," it is then said: "and the children of Israel kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month." For they could not "keep the Passover" before circumcision, nor eat the flesh of the lamb immediately after circumcision, before they were "healed." But after they "were healed," it is said that: "the children of Israel kept the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month." You see, then, that no one unclean "keeps the Passover," no one uncircumcised, but whoever is clean and circumcised, just as the Apostle also interprets it, saying: "for indeed Christ our Passover has been sacrificed. Therefore let us celebrate the feast, not with the old leaven, nor with the leaven of malice and wickedness, but with the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth." … But meanwhile, after Jesus led his people into the holy land, then, when all had been conquered, he celebrates the Passover.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote:
After they observed the Passover in Egypt, they began the exodus. In the book of Joshua, however, after the crossing of the Jordan, on the tenth day of the first month they encamped in Gilgal.…Then the sons of Israel observed the Passover on the fourteenth day of the month much more cheerfully than the one in Egypt, seeing that they also "ate unleavened bread and fresh from the grain of the holy land," a food better than the manna.
For God does not feed them on lesser foods when they have received the land according to promise, nor do they obtain inferior bread through Jesus [Joshua] who is so great. This will be clear to the one who has perceived the true holy land and the Jerusalem above.
source_title: COMMENTARY ON THE GOSPEL OF JOHN 6.233-35

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But at that time, indeed, when the people went out from the land of Egypt, "each carried, sprinkled in his garments," what was strewn. But when what was strewn had run out and they had no bread, God "rained down manna" for them. But when they came to the holy land and "took the fruits of the province of the palms," the "manna failed" them, and then they began to eat of the fruits of the land. And so three kinds of food are described in general. The first, indeed, is that on which we feed as we go out from the land of Egypt, but this suffices for a little time. After this, however, the manna succeeds. But the third we now "take" as "fruit" from the holy land. In which differences, as far as the understanding of my littleness reaches, I judge this to be indicated: that the first food, which we carried with us as we went out from Egypt, is this small schoolboy learning (or even, if perhaps someone has attained something of liberal letters), which can help us but a little. But placed in the desert — that is, in this state of life in which we now are — we feed on the manna through this, that we are instructed by the teachings of the divine law. But whoever has deserved to enter the "land of promise" — that is, to attain those things which have been promised by the Savior — he will eat the "fruits from the region of the palms." For truly he will find the "fruit of the palm" who, having overcome the enemy, has arrived at the things promised. For it is certain that, however great those things are which we can now understand or perceive in the law of God or in the divine writings, far more sublime and lofty will be those which, when the "riddle" ceases, all the saints will deserve to "see" "face to face," because "the things which eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor have ascended into the heart of man, these has God prepared for those who love him."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But see what fruits he first receives in the land of promise: then, it says, "they ate" first "of the fruits" from the region of palms, and "they ate" first "the unleavened bread." You see, therefore, that when we have first departed from the journey of this world, if we rightly follow Jesus, the first thing that meets us is the palm of victory, and, when the "leaven of malice and wickedness" has been cast away, the "unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" is prepared for us.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But if the law is to be understood according to the letter alone, the children of Israel will without doubt be found — when they were using better things, for they were taking manna from heaven — to have received worse things from the promise, whereas, when the Egyptian foods first failed them, a better food had succeeded, the manna from heaven. And how now will it be thought that, when the better food ceased, a worse succeeded, unless because a greater and truer meaning is grasped in the spiritual understanding than in the text of the letter?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But see what fruits he first receives in the land of promise: then, it says, "they ate" first "of the fruits" from the region of palms, and "they ate" first "the unleavened bread." You see, therefore, that when we have first departed from the journey of this world, if we rightly follow Jesus, the first thing that meets us is the palm of victory, and, when the "leaven of malice and wickedness" has been cast away, the "unleavened bread of sincerity and truth" is prepared for us.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And therefore one must beware and act carefully, so that you may knowingly discern the kind of visions, just as Joshua the son of Nun also, when he saw a vision, knowing that there was temptation in this, at once inquires of him who appeared and says: "Are you ours or of our adversaries?" So then the advancing soul also, when it has come to this point, that it now begins to have discernment of visions, will thereby be proved to be spiritual, if it knows how to discern all things. Finally, therefore, among the spiritual gifts as well, one of the gifts of the Holy Spirit is said to be the discernment of spirits.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "And it came to pass," it says, "when Jesus was at Jericho, that looking up with his eyes he saw a man standing over against him, and a drawn sword was in his hand. And Jesus, drawing near, said to him: are you ours, or of our adversaries? And he said: I am the prince of the host of the Lord's power; now I have come." "Looking up," then, "with his eyes he sees the prince of the Lord's host," as one who had not "looked up" before, but only then, when he was about to see the "prince of the Lord's host." Yet when Jesus had seen him, he did not see him as a common man, but understood that he was a certain power. Nevertheless he is not yet certain whether the one who appears is one from the divine powers or from the contrary ones, and therefore he asks and inquires, saying: "are you ours, or of our adversaries?"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: And he says: "I am the prince of the host of the Lord's power; now I have come." And when he had heard this, Jesus worshiped and said: "Lord, what do you command your servant?" What is it that Jesus teaches us through this? That, without doubt, which the Apostle says: "do not believe every spirit, but test whether it is of God." Jesus, then, recognized not only that "he is of God," but that he is God; for he would not have worshiped had he not recognized God. For who else is the "prince of the host of the Lord's powers" but our Lord Jesus Christ? For all the host of heaven, whether angels or archangels, or powers "or dominions or principalities or authorities," all these, which were made through him, do military service under him as prince, who is the prince of princes and who bestows principalities upon princes. For it is he who says in the Gospel: "be one having authority over ten cities," and to another: "be one having authority over five cities." It is he who, "having received the kingdom, returned."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But meanwhile let us see what the present reading suggests. Jesus is at Jericho; the enemies still hold the city and are not yet conquered. Yet already it is said to Jesus: "loose the shoe from your feet; for the place in which you stand is holy ground." And how is Jericho "holy ground," which is held by the enemies? But perhaps this is what is indicated: that wherever the "prince of the host of the Lord's power" comes, he sanctifies the place, because Jericho itself was not a holy place; but because the "prince of the Lord's host" came there, the place is called "holy." I even dare something further, and say that even where Moses stood, of itself it was not a holy place, but because the Lord stood with Moses, the presence of the Lord had sanctified the place, and therefore it is said to him: "loose the strap of your shoe: for the place in which you stand is holy ground." Whence we too, if by our life and merits we draw near to the Lord and are made worthy for God to stand by us, it is said also to us that we should loose from the feet of our soul whatever bond of mortality is bound to them. For these are the "feet" which Jesus "washes"; which, "unless he washes them, we shall have no part with him." So then, if we loose from our soul and senses every bond of mortal care, immediately God too will gladly be present and stand by us.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us see what it is that is indicated in what follows. For Jesus says: "keep yourselves from the accursed thing, lest perhaps you covet and take of the accursed thing, and make the camp of the children of Israel accursed, and crush yourselves and the whole synagogue of the Lord." Such is what is indicated in these words: see that you have nothing worldly in you, that you do not carry along with you into the church worldly ways, nor vices, nor the shiftiness of the world; but let all worldly conduct be "accursed" to you. Do not mix worldly things with divine, do not insert the business of the age into the secret things of the church. This is what John too sounds forth with the trumpet of his epistle, saying: "do not love the world, nor the things that are in the world." And Paul likewise: "do not," he says, "be conformed to this world." For those who do these things "take of the accursed thing." But also those who, for example, though they are Christians, celebrate the festivals of the nations, bring "the accursed thing" into the churches. Those who search out the lives and deeds of men from the courses of the stars, who inquire into the flights of birds and other things of this kind, which were formerly observed in the world, bring "the accursed thing" from Jericho into the church, and defile the camp of the Lord, and cause the people of God to be conquered. But there are also many other sins through which "the accursed thing" from Jericho is brought into the church; through which the people of God is conquered and laid low by its enemies. Or does not the Apostle also enjoin these very things when he says: "a little leaven corrupts the whole lump"?

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Jericho is overthrown by the trumpets of the priests. For at once, as soon as the blast of the trumpets sounded loudly, the whole circuit of walls was thrown down. We had already said before too that Jericho holds the figure of the present age, whose strength and defenses we see destroyed by the priestly trumpets. For the firmness and defenses which this world used as walls were the worship of idols, the deceit of divinations administered by the craft of demons, the fabrications of augurs and soothsayers and magicians — by all of which this world was fenced about as by the strongest walls. Moreover it was also fortified by the diverse doctrines of the philosophers and by the most lofty assertions of their disputations, as by certain tall and sturdy towers. But when our Lord Jesus Christ came, whose coming that former son of Nave prefigured, he sends his priests, the Apostles, bearing "trumpets of beaten metal," the magnificent and heavenly teaching of preaching. With the priestly trumpet Matthew first sounded loudly in his Gospel; Mark also, Luke, and John each sang with their priestly trumpets; Peter too resounds with the two trumpets of his epistles; James also and Jude. Nonetheless John also adds still further to sound the trumpet through his epistles, and Luke by describing the deeds of the Apostles. But last of all comes that one who said: "for I think that God has set forth us Apostles as the last," and, thundering in the trumpets of his fourteen epistles, he cast down to the very foundations the walls of Jericho and all the engines of idolatry and the doctrines of the philosophers.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: I am indeed also moved by this, which the narrative relates: that not only did the priests sound the trumpets so that the walls of Jericho might fall, but also that, "when the voice of the trumpet was heard," it is said that "the whole people howled with a great howling," or, as it stands in other copies, "shouted for joy with a great jubilation." And although this word may seem to have been improperly translated — for in the Greek it is written ἀλαλαγμός, which properly signifies neither jubilation nor howling, but rather denotes that shout by which, in time of war, an army raising a united cry is accustomed with one mind to exhort itself to battle — yet in the Scriptures this word is customarily written down as jubilation rather than as howling, as there: "shout for joy to the Lord, all the earth," and again: "blessed is the people that knows the jubilation." And this saying too moves me: what so great a work this is, that it "makes the people blessed." He did not say "blessed is the people" that works righteousness, or "blessed is the people" that knows the mysteries, or that knows the reckoning of heaven and earth and the stars, but he says, "blessed is the people that knows the jubilation." In other places the fear of God makes one blessed, but it makes only a single man blessed; for so it says: "blessed is the man that fears the Lord." Elsewhere too more are made blessed, such as the "poor in spirit," or the "meek," or the "peacemakers," or the "pure in heart." But this beatitude is lavished abroad, and by some cause of blessedness, I know not what, so great a thing is here indicated, that it makes the "whole people" alike "blessed" — the people, however, "that has known the jubilation." Hence it seems to me that this jubilation indicates a certain disposition of concord and unanimity. And if it should fall upon two or three of Christ's disciples, whatever they ask in the name of the Savior, the heavenly Father grants to them. But if the beatitude be so great that the whole people remains harmonious and of one mind, so that "all say the same thing, continuing in the same understanding and in the same judgment," then, when such a people lifts up its voice with one accord, there will come to pass that which is written in the Acts of the Apostles, that "there was a great earthquake," where at that time "the Apostles were praying with one accord together with the women and Mary the mother of Jesus"; and when the earthquake has occurred, all things that are earthly will be destroyed and will fall, and the world itself will be overturned. Hear, finally, our Lord and Savior exhorting his soldiers to this very thing, how he says: "be of good cheer, I have overcome the world." Under that leader, then, the world has already been overcome by us, and its walls have collapsed — the walls on which the men of the age relied. But each one of us too ought to accomplish these things within his very self. You have within you Jesus as your leader through faith; make for yourself "trumpets of beaten metal," if you are a priest; nay rather, since you are a priest — for you have been made a "royal race," and a "holy priesthood" has been spoken of concerning you — make for yourself "trumpets of beaten metal" out of the holy Scriptures; from there draw your meanings, from there your words; for it is on this account that they are called trumpets of beaten metal. Sound upon them, that is, "sing in psalms, in hymns, in spiritual songs," sound in the prophetic sacraments, in the mysteries of the law, in the apostolic doctrines. And if you sound upon such trumpets and carry the ark of the testament around "seven times," that is, if you do not separate the mystical precepts of the law from the evangelical trumpets, if you also exact from your very self the harmony of jubilation — that is, if the people of your thoughts and senses, which is within you, always utters a concordant and consonant voice, and you do not sometimes speak the truth and sometimes stain yourself with a lie by flattering a powerful person; if remissness does not at times make you fawning, and anger at times make you savage; if you are not found arrogant toward the lowly and humble before the proud; in short, if a battle is no longer waged within you while "the flesh lusts against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh" — if these things now sound in unison and are in concord within you, send forth the voice of jubilation, since for you the world has been destroyed and cast down. Such, I suppose, was also that man who confidently said: "but far be it from me to glory, save in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world has been crucified to me, and I to the world."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: Yet something in the passage still moves me: I seem to have perceived too little concerning the jubilation, to have said lowly things about great matters. At the coming of Jesus the walls of Jericho were overturned; at the coming of my Lord Jesus the world is conquered. Yet how the world is conquered, I would like to know more plainly and to understand more clearly the things that are said. I myself, who teach you, wish to learn together with you. Let us commonly take Paul to ourselves as our teacher; for he is the fellow-initiate of Christ, who can show us how Christ conquered the world. Hear him, then, saying: "that which was contrary to us, he took it out of the midst, nailing it to his cross; and stripping off the principalities and powers, he led them openly, triumphing over them on the wood of the cross." From these words, then, I understand this: that the heavenly powers, seeing the battle of Jesus, seeing the contrary "principalities and powers" stripped of their powers, seeing "the strong man bound and his vessels plundered," sounded their heavenly trumpets, because, when "the prince of this world" was bound, the world was conquered, and the heavenly army gave forth the voice of jubilation in the triumph of Christ. Truly, then, blessed is the people of the nations, which has come to know such a jubilation as this of the heavenly army, and which recognizes the mysteries and believes.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us see what things follow. Jericho is surrounded; it must be taken by storm. How, then, is Jericho stormed? No sword is drawn against it, no battering-ram is directed, nor are missiles hurled; only the priestly trumpets are employed, and by these the walls of Jericho are undermined. We frequently find in the Scriptures that Jericho is set down as a figure of this world. For in the Gospel too, that which is said, that "a man went down from Jerusalem to Jericho and fell among robbers," was without doubt an image of that Adam who was thrust from paradise into the exile of this world. And the "blind men" too, who were in Jericho, to whom Jesus came to make them see, bore the figure of those who in this world were pressed down by the blindness of ignorance, to whom the Son of God came. This Jericho, then — that is, this world — is to fall; for the consummation of the age has long since been made widely known in the sacred volumes. How, then, will its consummation be given? By what instruments? "By the voices," it says, "of the trumpets." Of which "trumpets"? Let Paul disclose to you the secret of this mystery; listen to what he himself says: "the trumpet shall sound," he says, "and the dead who are in Christ shall rise incorruptible," and: "the Lord himself, at the command, at the voice of the archangel, and at the trumpet of God, shall descend from heaven." Then, therefore, Jesus our Lord, with the trumpets, conquers Jericho and lays it low, so that from it the harlot alone is saved, and all her house.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: The consummation of the world will not happen in stages, but suddenly. With this ought to be compared, I think, what was written in Joshua, when by a single sound of a trumpet the crumbling city of Jericho suddenly perished; and like this example Babylon also in the consummation of the age will fall and suddenly be obliterated.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us now see the things that follow. Jericho having been overturned, Rahab the harlot alone is saved. For thus it is written of her: "and Rahab the harlot and all the house of her father, Jesus made alive; and she was joined to Israel unto this present day." I would like to inquire of the Jews, and of those who are indeed called Christians but still keep a Jewish sense in the Scriptures, how they explain that "Rahab the harlot was joined to the house of Israel unto this present day." How is Rahab said to be "joined unto this present day"? For it is the custom of holy Scripture to say this of those things which remain unto the end either of life or of the age. For example, as it says: "this is the father of the Moabites unto this present day," which signifies unto the end of the age. And again in the Gospel it is said that "this saying was spread abroad among the Jews unto this present day," that is, as long as the age stands. But how is Rahab, a woman, said to be "joined to the house of Israel unto this present day"? Is a succession of posterity ascribed to a mother, so that she may seem to be preserved in the renewal of offspring? Or is it rather to be understood that she "has been joined" and made a companion to the true Israel "unto this present day"? And if you wish to see more plainly how "Rahab is joined to Israel," look at how "the branch of the wild olive is grafted into the root of the good olive tree," and you will understand how those who have been grafted into the faith of Abraham and Isaac and Jacob are rightly said to be "set beside" and "joined to Israel unto this present day," because in their "root" we, "the branches of the wild olive" taken from among the nations — we who once played the harlot, worshiping "wood and stone" in place of the true God — "have been set beside them unto this present day," and, on account of faith in Christ, we have been made "above," while that people which has remained unbelieving has been made "below," according to the prophecy of Deuteronomy. If anyone, then, has within himself Christ, who is "the head of all," this one is made "into the head"; for they denied Christ Jesus and were made into the tail, and those who were "first" have been made "last."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "The Lord" our Jesus "shall come," then, "and shall come at the voice of the trumpets." But even now let us pray that he may come and destroy this "world," which "is set in wickedness," and "all the things that are in the world," because "everything that is in the world is the lust of the flesh and the lust of the eyes." May he destroy those things, may he now, this very moment, dissolve them, but may he save this one alone, who received his spies, who received his Apostles in faith and obedience and set them in the upper rooms, and may he join and unite this harlot with the house of Israel. But let us now not bring up again nor reckon against her the old fault. Once she was a harlot, but now she is joined as "a chaste virgin to one husband, Christ." Hear the Apostle saying of her: "for I have determined this very thing, to present you as a chaste virgin to one husband, Christ." From her too was that very one who said: "for we also were once foolish, unbelieving, going astray, serving desires and various pleasures." Do you wish to learn yet more fully how the harlot is now no longer a harlot? Hear Paul saying further: "and such indeed you were; but you have been washed, but you have been sanctified in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and in the Spirit of our God." For that she might be able to escape, lest she perish with Jericho, she received from the spies a most powerful "sign" of salvation, the "scarlet cord." For through the blood of Christ this whole Church is saved, in Christ himself our Lord, "to whom is glory and dominion unto ages of ages. Amen!"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But this too must not be run over idly: that when one man sinned, wrath came upon the whole people. How does this happen? When the priests, who are set over the people, wish to seem kindly toward wrongdoers, and, fearing the tongues of sinners lest perhaps they speak ill of them, forgetful of priestly severity, are unwilling to fulfill what is written: "rebuke the sinner before all, that the rest may have fear," and again: "take away the evil from among your own selves," nor, kindled with zeal for God, do they imitate the Apostle who says that "such a man is to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, that the spirit may be saved." Nor do they strive to fulfill that evangelical precept that, if they see one sinning, they should first meet him privately, afterward also with "two or three witnesses"; and if he shall have despised this and after the church's correction shall not have been amended, they should hold him, expelled from the church, "as a heathen and a publican." And while they spare one, they contrive the ruin of the whole church. What kind of goodness is this, what kind of mercy is it, to spare one and to bring all into danger? For the people is defiled by one sinner. Just as by one diseased sheep the whole flock is infected, so also, when one man either fornicates or commits any other kind of crime, the whole populace is defiled. And therefore let us watch over one another, and let the conduct of each one be known, especially to the priests and ministers. Nor let them think they are speaking rightly when they say: what does this concern me, if another does evil? This is to say, as the head says to the feet: what does it pertain to me, if my feet ache, if they are in a bad state? it is no concern of mine, so long as the head continues in health; or as if the eye should say to the hand: I do not need your work, what does it pertain to me if you ache, if you are wounded? shall I, the eye, be troubled by the sickness of the hand? Such, then, is what those do who preside over the churches, not considering that we who believe are all "one body," having one God, who binds us together in unity and holds us fast, namely Christ, of whose body you, who preside over the church, are the eye — for this very purpose, surely, that you may look around upon all things, survey all things, and even foresee things to come. You are a shepherd; you see the little sheep of the Lord, unaware of the danger, being carried to the precipices and hanging over the crags: do you not run to meet them? do you not call them back? do you not at least restrain them with your voice and deter them with the shout of rebuke? Are you so forgetful of the Lord's sacrament that, whereas he, "having left the ninety-nine in the heavens" for the sake of one little sheep "that had gone astray," descended to the earth and, having found it, "carried it back upon his shoulders" to heaven, we in no way at all follow the example of the master shepherd in caring for the little sheep? We do not say these things in order that anyone should be cut off for a slight fault; but if perhaps someone, having been admonished and rebuked for his offense once and again and a third time, has shown no amendment, let us use the discipline of the physician. If we have anointed with oil, if we have soothed with plasters, if we have softened with a poultice, and yet the hardness of the swelling does not yield to the medicines, the only remaining remedy is to cut it away. For so the Lord also says: "if your right hand causes you to stumble, cut it off and cast it away from you." Does the hand of our body ever "cause us to stumble," or is it about this hand of the body that the Gospel says: "cut it off, and cast it away from you"? But this is what it means: that I, who seem to you to be the right hand and am named a presbyter and seem to preach the word of God, if I do anything against ecclesiastical discipline and the rule of the Gospel, so that I cause a stumbling-block to you, to the church, then the whole church, conspiring together in one consent, should cut me off as its right hand and cast me away from itself. For "it is expedient for you," the church, without me, your hand — who by doing evil "have caused a stumbling-block" — to enter into the kingdom of heaven, rather than with me "to go into hell." We have said these things for this reason, because we see it related in the holy Scriptures that on account of one man sinning "the children of Israel were made accursed," so that they were conquered by their enemies.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us also see what his very sin was: "he stole," it says, "a tongue of gold, and placed it in his tent." I do not think that in that theft of a little gold there was such force of sin that it could stain so innumerable a church of the Lord. But let us see whether perhaps, in the inner understanding, the bitterness of this sin is so great and so grave. There is much beauty in words, and much loveliness in the discourses of the philosophers or the rhetoricians, who are all from the city of Jericho, that is, men of this world. If, then, you find among the philosophers perverse doctrines adorned with the assertions of brilliant speech, this is "the tongue of gold." But see that the splendor of the work does not deceive you, that the beauty of golden speech does not carry you away; remember that Jesus commanded all the gold that should be found in Jericho to be "accursed." If you read a poet weaving gods and goddesses in measured verses and in resplendent song, do not be delighted by the sweetness of eloquence: for it is a tongue of gold; if you take it up and place it in your tent, if you bring into your heart the things that are asserted by them, you will defile the whole church of the Lord. This the wretched Valentinus did, and Basilides; this Marcion also did. These men stole "tongues of gold" from Jericho and attempted to introduce into the churches the not-upright sects of the philosophers and to defile the whole church of the Lord. But let us follow the preceding example of the fathers; let us examine more diligently, lest anyone should have a Jerichoan "tongue" hidden in his tent, and let us cast away the evil from our very selves, because, even if we hold back, God will convict him, so that he himself will spontaneously confess and say: "I stole a tongue of gold and pure bracelets." Do you see of what sort was the theft he stole? He steals "a tongue" and "pure bracelets." Now "pure bracelets" are works in which nothing divine is mixed, but the whole is carried out according to man. Indeed, in our disputations too it is customary to say that we do not call Christ a mere man, but confess him God and man. But that which is stolen from Jericho is said to be "pure," that is, without God — which, for the one stealing it, was surely the cause of sin. And therefore let us perceive nothing pure and human concerning Christ, but let us confess him God and man alike, because the "wisdom" of God is also called "manifold," so that through these things we may deserve to take a share in "the wisdom of God," which is "Christ" Jesus our Lord, "to whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: When these things have been heard, it is likely that the hearers will say: what is this to me? What does it profit me if I come to know that those who inhabited Ai were conquered, as though similar or even more powerful wars had not been waged or are not being waged? Was this the care of the Holy Spirit, that, leaving aside the destructions of so many and so great and noble cities, the battle of the city of Ai should be written and consigned to the sacred volumes? Perhaps what we are doing is rash, in that we attempt to explain places of Holy Scripture so lofty and so difficult; but if you aid us with your prayers, we shall not only escape the fault of audacity, but also God the Father of the Word, embracing our devotion, "will give a word for the opening of our mouth," whereby both you may be edified and we may appear not undevout. Praying, therefore, and attentive in mind, listen. First, because of our sins we were conquered, and those who inhabited Ai slew a great many of us. Ai is interpreted "Chaos." But we know that Chaos is the place or dwelling of the contrary powers, whose king and prince is the devil. Coming against him, Jesus divides the people into two parts, and some indeed he stations in the front, others in the rear, who may come unexpectedly upon the backs of the enemy. And see whether that is not the first part of the people, of which he says: "I have not come except to the lost sheep of the house of Israel," and of which the Apostle says: "but grace and peace to every man who works good, to the Jew first, then also to the Greek," that is, to the Gentile who comes after. This, then, is the people who is stationed in front and, as it were, flees with Jesus. But the latter people is the one which is gathered from the nations, and which, coming unexpectedly — for who would have hoped that the nations would be saved? — cuts down the adversaries the more fiercely from behind; and thus each people lays low and conquers the throng of demons enclosed in the middle.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: We entreat you, O hearers of the sacred volumes, not to listen with weariness or distaste to the things that are read, on the ground that their narrative seems to be less delightful. For you ought to know that the things which are read are indeed worthy of the utterance of the Holy Spirit, but for explaining them we have need of that grace of the Holy Spirit of which the Apostle speaks: "to one, moreover, is given through the Spirit the word of wisdom, to another the word of knowledge according to the same Spirit." We too, then, have need of these things in the present passages, in which it is related that Jesus succeeded Moses, and that he himself leads the people, and a certain such history is prefigured in the present reading. Those who inhabited the city of Ai at first seemed indeed to conquer and to turn back the sons of Israel because of the sin which they had committed. But afterward, when the evil had been removed from their midst, Jesus, the leader of the people, is commanded by God to divide the people into two parts, so that one part should feign flight, while the other part should lie waiting in ambush, by which Ai might be deceived when Jesus should give the command. When these things had been thus arranged, "the king of Ai, seeing" Jesus and the sons of Israel from afar, "is stirred up against them into battle." And when the former feigned flight, the others pursue them the more fiercely, and, as though about to carry off spoils from the enemy, all together "go forth out of the city," so that, as Scripture says, "they left the city empty." But after they had advanced to the appointed place, Jesus turned and gave a signal that "those who were in the ambushes should rise up" and cut down the backs of the enemy; and thus those who were last and these who were first slay all the enemy enclosed in the middle. And in this manner, when those who inhabited Ai had been conquered, "they hanged" their "king upon a double wood."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But perhaps you may say to me: how, then, is the former people set as though fleeing? And quite consistently. For those who follow Jesus were seen to flee from the legal burdens and precepts, from the observance of the sabbath, from the circumcision of the flesh, from the slaughter of victims. But again he who has followed Christ, the perfection and fullness of the law, does not flee.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But something else also occurs to me as I consider in this place "Jesus fleeing from the face" of the army of Ai. What do you think it is that "Jesus fleeing" signified? Let us see whether perhaps there is something which we conquer by fleeing, and there is some perfect virtue in flight. Paul the Apostle teaches us, saying: "flee fornication." You see, then, that there is a certain "spirit of fornication," which we ought to flee, whoever of us wishes to remain chastely and piously and modestly in Christ. This flight, then, is the one which has salvation; this flight is of virtue; this flight confers blessedness. And not only is the spirit of fornication to be fled, but in like manner, just as it was said, "flee fornication," let us hear it said to us: flee anger, flee avarice, flee envy and spite, flee detractions and evil-speakings. And yet I know not whether anyone escapes these, I know not whether anyone gets away. Such was that army of Ai, which Jesus taught his soldiers to flee, and concerning these perhaps he commands his disciples, saying: "if they persecute you in this city, flee into another; and if in another, flee into another." For he wishes us to flee from enemies of this kind, he wishes us to be made far from evils of this kind; and if in the meanwhile we can escape the contagions of these evils by fleeing, then, seeing the devotion and the purpose of our mind, certain holy virtues — those perhaps of which the Apostle Paul says: "are they not all ministering spirits sent forth into ministry for the sake of those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?" — who perhaps are the holy angels, who, seeing us suffer the pursuit of the demons, rise up against those who pursue us and, cutting them all down from behind, slay them. For Jesus is with those who suffer pursuit, rather than with those who persecute. And rightly, because Jesus delights to be with those who "flee fornication," who flee pride, who flee deceit, and who flee falsehood. If, then, we thus understand the things which are written, the reading will perhaps seem worthy of the pen of the Holy Spirit. For what does it profit me if I know that "the king of Ai was hanged upon a double wood"? But if I know that the virtue of the cross is twofold, on which both Christ is hanged in the flesh and the devil with his army is triumphed over, from the understanding of the sacrament my soul will be edified. And still more perhaps, that we may extend the breadth of the mystery yet more loftily, in this wood is understood to be "the knowledge of good and evil," on which both the good Christ and the evil devil hung, but the evil one indeed that he might perish, and the good one that he might live from power; as the Apostle also says concerning Christ, that "even if he was crucified from weakness, yet he lives from the power of God." Nay, not only that he might live, but that he might give life, because he is "the last Adam unto a life-giving spirit." But these things must be understood to be said figuratively; for Christ himself is called "the tree of life." But just as in other passages he is shown to be both priest and victim and altar, and the one meaning is not hindered by the other, but each single thing is understood figuratively concerning him in its own places, so also now in the figures of the sacraments the diversity of persons taken up concerning one and the same thing will not hinder.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us see what is also written in what follows: "and they struck them," he says, "with the edge of the sword, until there was not left of them one who might be saved, nor who might escape." When the Jews read these things, they become cruel and thirst for human blood, thinking that the saints too struck those who inhabited Ai, so that "there should not be left of them one who might be saved, nor who might escape," not understanding that in these words mysteries are foreshadowed, and that this is rather indicated to us, that of these whose dwelling is chaos and who reigned in the abyss, of the demons, we ought to leave none at all, but to slay them all. But we slay the demons not by destroying their very substance; but because their work and their zeal is this, to make men sin, and this is their life, if we sin, without doubt it is their destruction, if we do not sin. Therefore the saints slay the inhabitants of Ai and destroy them and do not let go one of them — those, without doubt, who with all diligence guard their heart, lest "evil thoughts proceed" from it; but also those who watch over their mouth, so that "every evil word may not proceed from" their "mouth": this is "to leave none who might escape," when no evil word escapes them either. Come, then, you too, let us prepare ourselves for battles of this kind, let us strike Ai "with the edge of the sword" and extinguish all who inhabit chaos, all the contrary powers. Would that I too, even now, while I speak the word of God to you, might be able to strike the heart of the sinner! For if I do so, it is certain that with the "sword of my mouth" I shall strike fornication, I shall strike malice, I shall repress fury and, if there are any other evils, "with the edge of the sword," that is, with the speech of my mouth, I shall quench them and "shall not leave of them one who might be saved, nor who might escape." For if we extinguish all these enemies of ours, then we shall truly celebrate a feast day to God and, our adversaries being vanquished, we shall rejoice with glad solemnity. Some such thing seems to me to be signified also by the holy prophet in the psalms, where he says of himself that "in the mornings I slew all the sinners of the earth, that I might destroy from the city of the Lord all who work iniquity." For whether "the city of the Lord" is taken to be the church of the living God, the teachers cast out from the church and slay those "who work iniquity," the contrary demons and the adversary powers, who compel men to sin by teaching, by instructing, and by unlocking the mysteries hidden in the divine letters from such places as those in which we now are; or whether by "the city of the Lord" we understand the soul of each one of us, which is built by the Lord from "living stones," that is, from various and diverse virtues: from that city too every holy and diligent man casts out "the sinners," that is, "slays in the morning" the worst thoughts and depraved desires. For the just man says: "in the mornings I meditated on you, because you were my helper." What is this "morning," except our Lord Jesus Christ, who is "the true light" and "rising in our hearts" and illuminating the darkness of our ignorance and revealing to us mysteries of this kind, makes us "see light in his light"? If ever, then, you read in the holy scriptures of the battles of the just, the slaughters and the massacres of the slain, and that the saints spare none at all of the enemy — nay rather, that even if they had spared, "it is reckoned to them as sin," just as "it was reckoned" to Saul, who "had preserved alive Agag king of Amalek" — understand the wars of the just in this manner in which we have expounded above, because these wars are waged by them against sin. But how will the just remain, if they have reserved even some little of sin in themselves? And therefore it is said of these that "they left not even one who might be saved or escape." Perhaps you may not believe me that a battle is enjoined upon us against sin; believe Paul, who says: "you have not yet resisted unto blood against sin." You see that a battle "against sin" is set before you, and that this fight is to be consummated "unto the shedding of blood"? Or does not the divine Scripture indicate these things evidently, in those places too where it is its custom to say: "sanctify a war" and: "you shall fight the fight of the Lord"? For what else is it "to sanctify a war," except, when all the enemies of our soul, which are the vices of sins, have been slain, and "the members which are upon the earth having been mortified" and all evil desires cut off, to be made "holy in body and spirit" and, acting bravely, to come to the sight of the living God and to be crowned by Christ Jesus our Lord for the palm of the victory of virtue by merit? "To whom is glory and dominion unto the ages of ages. Amen!"

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But let us see what follows in the sequel: "and Jesus burned Ai," he says, "and it was made a wasteland, that it should not be inhabited forever." You see that these things which follow pertain more to the truth of the mystery than of the history. For that place of earth is not so much uninhabitable forever as the place of the demons will then be uninhabitable, when now no one will sin, "neither will sin reign" in anyone, when the devil and his angels will be delivered to eternal fire, our Lord Jesus Christ sitting as king and judge and saying to those who conquered, both the first and the last: "come, blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom which has been prepared for you by my Father." But to the others he will say: "go into the eternal fire, which God has prepared for the devil and his angels," until he takes counsel with remedies for every soul, for those whom he himself knows, and "all Israel is made safe."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But after all things, even "the king of Ai" is said "to be hanged upon a double wood." In this place a mystery is concealed which lies hidden from very many, but, with you praying, we shall attempt to open these things not by our own opinions, but by the testimonies of divine Scripture. In the foregoing we said that the king of Ai may be compared to the devil; here it is worth the effort to know how "he is crucified upon a double wood." The cross of our Lord Jesus Christ was double. Perhaps what I say seems to you a strange and novel saying: that the cross was double, that is, it consists of a twofold and double reasoning; because visibly indeed the Son of God was crucified in the flesh, but invisibly upon that cross the devil with "his principalities and powers was affixed to the cross." Will this not seem true to you if I produce for you the Apostle Paul as witness of these things? Hear, then, what he himself declares concerning these things: "that which was," he says, "contrary to us, he took it away out of the midst, affixing it to his cross, and stripping the principalities and powers he displayed them openly, triumphing over them on the wood of the cross" — although in other copies it is found: "triumphing over them in himself," but among the Greeks it is found "on the wood." Therefore the reasoning of the Lord's cross is twofold: one, that by which the Apostle Peter says that "Christ, crucified, left us an example," and this second, by which that "cross" was a trophy over the devil, "on which he was both crucified and triumphed over." Therefore, finally, the Apostle Paul also said: "but far be it from me to glory except in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ, through whom the world is crucified to me and I to the world." You see that here too the Apostle has set forth a twofold reasoning of the cross. For he says that two things contrary to each other were crucified, himself holy and the world sinful, after that likeness, without doubt, which we spoke of above, of Christ and the devil. For we are "crucified to the world" then, when "the prince of this world, coming, finds nothing in us"; and "the world is crucified to us," when we do not receive the concupiscences of sin.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But if perchance there is some more attentive hearer, he can say: the form of the things done seems indeed to be fitting, but this still troubles me, that the devil and his army, as far as is shown by the figure of the history, was destroyed; and how do we still see both the devil and the contrary powers to prevail so greatly against the servants of God, that even the Apostle Peter with great caution forewarns and says that it must be observed that "our adversary the devil goes about like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour"? Let us see, therefore, whether in this too we can find something worthy of the utterances of the Holy Spirit. One coming of Christ was accomplished in lowliness, but another is hoped for in glory; and this first coming in the flesh is, by a certain mystical manner of speech, in the holy scriptures called his "shadow," just as the prophet Jeremiah also announces, saying: "the spirit of our countenance, Christ the Lord, of whom we said: in his shadow we shall live among the nations." But Gabriel too, when he brought Mary the good tidings concerning his nativity, says: "the power of the Most High shall overshadow you." Wherefore we understand that very many things are foreshadowed at this first coming of his, whose fulfillment and perfection is consummated at the second coming. And the Apostle Paul says that "he raised us up together with him, and made us sit together in the heavenly places." And yet we do not yet see believers either already "raised up" or "seated together in the heavenly places," but these things are indeed now foreshadowed through faith, because in mind and hope we are lifted up from earthly and dead works and we raise our heart to heavenly and eternal things; yet this will be fulfilled at his second coming, so that the things which we now have anticipated by faith and hope, we may then also hold bodily by the actual accomplishment. So, then, concerning the devil also it must be understood that he was indeed conquered and crucified, but for those who have been crucified with Christ; but for all believers and for all the peoples alike he will then be crucified, when that shall be fulfilled which the Apostle says, that "as in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive." There is therefore in this also the mystery of the future resurrection. For then too the people will be divided into two parts, there will then also be some first and others last, who, when they have conspired together into one under Jesus, then already the devil shall no longer be at all, because "there shall no more be death." Do you wish that we prove these things to you also by divine testimonies? Hear the Apostle saying: "for this we say to you in the word of the Lord, that we who live, who are left, at the coming of the Lord shall not precede those who have fallen asleep, because the Lord himself, at the command, at the voice of the archangel and at the trumpet of God, shall descend from heaven, and the dead who are in Christ shall rise first, then we who live, who are left, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and so we shall always be with the Lord." And speaking about the devil he says: "the last enemy that is destroyed is death," because then death is truly "conquered," when "this mortal is swallowed up by life."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After Jesus had overthrown Ai, that is, chaos, and had removed all its inhabitants, it was fitting that he should offer to God, the Most High over all, some gift worthy of so great and mighty a victory. Let us see, then, what this is that he does after the victory: "Jesus," it says, "built an altar to the Lord God of Israel on Mount Ebal, and he made it just as Moses the servant of the Lord commanded the children of Israel. Now it is written in the law of Moses that the altar should be made of whole stones, on which no iron has been laid." And after "Jesus made the altar," he placed "there whole burnt offerings to the Lord and offered a sacrifice of salvation," and after the sacrifice "Jesus wrote upon the stones the Deuteronomy, the law of Moses, and he wrote it in the presence of the children of Israel. And all the elders of Israel and the judges and their scribes went before, on this side and on that, the ark of the covenant of the Lord." Let us see, then, what is indicated in all these things, and what edification the present reading may gain for us. All of us who believe in Christ Jesus are called "living stones," according to what Scripture declares, saying: "But you are living stones, built up into a spiritual house in a holy priesthood, that you may offer spiritual victims, acceptable to God through Jesus Christ." Now, just as we know it is observed among these earthly stones that those stones which are stronger and more powerful are laid first in the foundations, so that the weight of the whole building may be entrusted to them and set upon them, while others which follow, that is, a little inferior to those, are arranged next to those which are in the foundation; and those which are still lower are set a little above the foundations, and then in turn those which are weaker, in comparison to those stones, are placed in the upper parts and now near the very peaks of the roof — so now understand also concerning the "living stones," that some of them are in the foundations of this spiritual building. But who are these that are placed in the foundations? "The apostles and prophets." For thus Paul speaks, teaching this very thing: "built," he says, "upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets, Christ Jesus our Lord himself being the cornerstone." But that you may prepare yourself more readily, O hearer, for the construction of this building, so that you may be found some stone nearer to the foundation, learn that Christ himself is also the foundation of this building which we are now describing. For thus says the Apostle Paul: "For no one can lay another foundation besides that which has been laid, which is Christ Jesus." Blessed, therefore, are those who build religious and holy edifices upon that so noble a foundation. But in this building of the Church there must also be an altar. Hence I judge that whoever among you "living stones" are fit for this and ready, so as to devote themselves to prayers, so as to offer supplications to God day and night and to sacrifice the victims of entreaties — these are the very ones from whom "Jesus builds an altar."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But observe what praise is ascribed to those very stones of the altar. "Just as," it says, "the lawgiver Moses said, that the altar should be built of whole stones, on which no iron has been laid." Who do you think are these "whole stones"? The conscience of each one knows who is whole, who is uncorrupted, unpolluted, unstained in flesh and in spirit, who is that one on whom "no iron has been laid," that is, who has not received "the flaming darts of the evil one" of concupiscence, but has "quenched" them with "the shield of faith" and driven them back; or who is that one who has never received the iron of strife, the iron of war, the iron of quarrels, but has always been peaceable, always quiet and gentle, formed by the humility of Christ. These, then, are the "living stones" from which Jesus our Lord "built an altar of whole stones, on which no iron has been laid," that he might offer upon them "whole burnt offerings and a sacrifice of salvation." I think that perhaps such "whole" and uncontaminated stones as these may be the holy apostles, all together making one altar because of their unanimity and concord. For thus they are reported all together, unanimously "praying" and opening their mouth to have "said": "You, Lord, who know the hearts of all." These, then, who were able unanimously, with one voice and one spirit, to pray, are perhaps themselves worthy, who ought all together to "build one altar," upon which Jesus may offer "a sacrifice" to the Father. Yet let us too try to give diligence, "that we may all say the same thing," "unanimous, of one mind, doing nothing through contention or through vainglory," but "remaining in one perception and in the same judgment," if perhaps we too may be made stones fit for the altar. For Jesus our Lord does not desert us, but although we, devoting ourselves to prayer, "know not what we should pray for as we ought, yet the Spirit himself intercedes for us with unspeakable groanings." "Now the Lord is a Spirit." If, then, the "Spirit" aids our prayers and offers them to the Father, the God of all, with "groanings" which we cannot express, it is certain that he also carefully requires of us the construction of an altar.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: But the adornment of the altar is not yet complete, even if it be built "of whole stones," even if "iron" and "the dart of the evil one" be not found "laid" upon them, but there is still something lacking, and there is still what Jesus may add to all these. What is it? "Jesus wrote," it says, "upon the stones of the altar the Deuteronomy, the law of Moses, and he wrote it in the sight of the children of Israel." As for the "writing" — however the son of Nave was then able to inscribe "the law upon the stones of the altar," and, as far as he was able, to sketch out the types: let us for our part see how our Jesus "wrote the Deuteronomy on the living and whole stones." Deuteronomy is so called as it were a second legislation. If, then, you wish to see how, the first law having been weakened, Jesus writes a second law, hear him saying in the Gospels: "It was said to the men of old: You shall not kill. But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother is a murderer"; and again: "It was said to the men of old: You shall not commit adultery. But I say to you, if anyone looks upon a woman to lust after her, he has already committed adultery with her in his heart"; and "It was said to the men of old: You shall not swear falsely. But I say to you: Do not swear at all." You see the "Deuteronomy" which "Jesus wrote on the living and whole stones," "not on tablets of stone, but on the fleshly tablets of the heart, not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God." But if you wish to know more clearly on which hearts "Jesus has written the law" and on which he has not written it, this too I will make plain to you from the authority of the Scriptures, that you who have been called from the Gentiles may take consolation, and may not fear the boasting of those who glory that they have received the law of Moses written on tablets or "little scrolls." Hear, then, in whose hearts the Lord Jesus has written the law. Paul says: "For when the Gentiles, who do not have the law, do by nature the things which are of the law, these, not having the law, are a law unto themselves. They show the work of the law written in their hearts, their conscience bearing witness to them." If, then, you see Gentiles coming to Jesus and believing in him and fulfilling the work of the law, which those who had received the law cannot fulfill, do not hesitate to say of them that "Jesus has written the Deuteronomy on those whole stones."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: I am indeed moved by what Scripture added in what follows. "And Jesus wrote," it says, "upon the stones the Deuteronomy in the presence of the children of Israel." How he could have "inscribed" so great a book while the "children of Israel" were standing by and remaining there, so that they did not depart until the writing of so many lines was finished, or even how the stones of the altar could have borne the contents of so great a book — let these Jewish defenders of the letter, who are ignorant of the spirit of the law, tell me. How is the truth of the history demonstrated in this? But among them "to this very day, when Moses is read, a veil is placed over their heart." But for us, "having turned to the Lord" Jesus, "the veil is taken away," because "where the Spirit of the Lord is, there is liberty" of understanding. Our Lord Jesus, then, does not need much time to write the Deuteronomy, to fix the second law in the hearts of believers, and to seal the law of the spirit in the minds of those who are worthy to be chosen for the construction of the altar. For as soon as anyone has believed in Jesus Christ, the law of the Gospel is inscribed in his heart, and inscribed "in the sight of the children of Israel." For there were present, when the sacrament of faith was being handed over to you, the heavenly powers, the ministries of angels, "the church of the firstborn." For if we rightly understand Israel to mean "a mind seeing God," this is most rightly said rather of the ministering angels, according to the saying of the Lord, who says of the little ones — and you too were a little one in baptism — that "their angels always see the face of my Father who is in heaven." "In the presence," therefore, of these "children of Israel," who were present at that time when the sacraments of faith were being handed over to you, "seeing the face of God," "Jesus wrote the Deuteronomy" in your heart. Do you wish that we prove this to you still more clearly from the holy Scriptures, that "in the presence of the children of Israel Jesus wrote the second law"? The Apostle to the Hebrews plainly designates it, saying: "For you have not come to the sound of the trumpet and the burning mountain, but you have come to Mount Zion and the city of the living God, the heavenly Jerusalem, and the church of the firstborn enrolled in heaven, and a multitude of angels praising God together." You see, then, that in the presence of all these, who from this — that they always see God — are deservedly called "children of Israel," "Jesus wrote his law" in the hearts of believers. But even now, through these things which we speak, "Jesus writes the Deuteronomy" in the hearts of those who with whole faith and whole soul receive the things that are said, who with whole hearing and whole heart, and with a sense not corrupt nor reprobate concerning the faith, hear and retain the things that are said, because it is necessary that "the Deuteronomy be written on whole stones."

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: After these things it says: "and all Israel," it says, "and the presbyters and the judges and the scribes went before, on this side and on that, the ark of the covenant of the Lord." "The ark of the covenant of the Lord" is that in which the tablets of the law, written by the hand of God, are kept. And around this "ark of the covenant" everyone who is "truly Israel" walks and is not far from it; but the Levites and priests even carry it upon their shoulders. For whoever live in priestly religion and holiness — not only those who seem to sit in the priestly assembly, but rather those who act in a priestly manner, whose "portion is the Lord" and who hold no share on earth — these are truly the priests and Levites of the Lord, who carry the law of God upon their shoulders, that is, by doing and fulfilling through their work the things that are written in the law.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "But both the proselyte," it says, "and the native-born together, and half were beside Mount Gerizim and half beside Mount Ebal." How shall we explain these things also? Truly there is need of the help of God, that we may be able with our words to expound and set forth the divine words: who are the "half" who walked "beside Gerizim," and who are the "half" who, although they too are saved, could nevertheless not walk "beside Mount Gerizim," but walk "beside Mount Ebal." "Mount Gerizim" holds the blessings, but "Mount Ebal" the curses which threaten sinners. For "they appointed," as it is written in Deuteronomy, six tribes "for blessing on Mount Gerizim" — and these the tribes which are more noble and choice, that is, "Simeon, Levi, Judah, Issachar, Joseph, and Benjamin" — but the other six, more ignoble ones, "for cursing," among which was also "Reuben," who "went up to his father's bed and defiled his father's couch," and "Zebulun," who is the last son of Leah.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: These things indeed the histories of the ancients relate as deeds done; but how shall we refer this narration of the history to a mystical understanding, so as to show who these are who walk "beside Mount Gerizim" and who these are who walk "beside Mount Ebal"? I see it thus, that there are two kinds of those who through faith hasten and press on toward salvation: one kind of those who, kindled by desire for the heavenly promises, strive with the utmost zeal and diligence, lest even the least beatitude should pass them by, having a longing not only to receive the blessing and "to be made a part of the lot of the saints," but also to stand in the sight of God and to be always with the Lord. But there are others who also themselves press toward salvation, but are not so much inflamed with love of the blessings or with desires for the promises as they rather hold this before their view, saying: it is enough for me not to go into Gehenna, it is enough for me not to be sent into the eternal fire, it is enough for me not to be cast out into the "outer darkness." Since, then, in each of the faithful there is such a variety of purpose, this seems to me to be signified in this place: that those "half" who walk "beside Mount Gerizim," which was chosen for the blessings, figuratively indicate those who come to salvation not from fear of punishment, but from desire of the blessings and the promises; while those "half" who walk "beside Mount Ebal," on which the curses were pronounced, indicate those others who, fulfilling from fear of evils and dread of punishments the things that are written in the law, arrive at salvation. Here now it belongs to God alone to know, out of all of us children of Israel, who is the one who, kindled with the desire of the good itself, does what is good, and who among us tends toward the good from fear of Gehenna and dread of the eternal fire, and is zealous and hastens to fulfill the things that are written. For it is certain that those are more noble who do what is good from desire of the good itself and from love of the blessings, than those who pursue the good for fear of evil. Jesus alone, therefore, is the one who can discern out of the whole people minds and spirits of this kind, and can set some indeed "on Mount Gerizim for the blessings," but others "set on Mount Ebal for the curses" — not that they may receive curses, but that, beholding the curses prescribed and the punishments appointed for sinners, they may take care to avoid them.

author: Origen of Alexandria
quote: "After these things" it is related that "Jesus read all the words of the law, the blessings and the curses, according to all that is written in the book of the law; nor was there any word out of all that Moses commanded which Jesus did not read in the presence of the whole assembly of the children of Israel." Easy indeed is the explanation of the history, how the son of Nave "read all the words of the law which Moses wrote, in the presence of the whole assembly of the children of Israel"; but how our Lord Jesus does this for his people, it does not seem to me idle to show. And I for my part judge that, "whenever Moses is read" to us and, through the grace of the Lord, "the veil of the letter is removed" and we begin to understand that "the law is spiritual," and that, for example, the law when it says "you shall not muzzle the mouth of the ox that treads out the grain" said this not about oxen, but about the apostles, and again, when it is said in the law "that Abraham had two sons, one of the handmaid and one of the free woman," I understand in these that there are two testaments and two peoples: this law, which is thus understood — which Paul names "spiritual" — "Jesus" the Lord "reads," and it is he who recites these things in the ears of the whole people, charging us not to follow "the letter that kills," but to hold to "the spirit that gives life." "Jesus," then, "reads" the law to us, when he reveals to us the hidden things of the law. For we who are of the catholic Church do not despise the law of Moses, but receive it, provided that "Jesus reads" it to us. For thus we shall be able rightly to understand the law, if "Jesus reads" it to us, so that, with him reading it, we may grasp its sense and understanding. Or is it not to be thought that he had conceived his understanding from thence, he who said: "But we have the mind of Christ, that we may know the things that have been given to us by God, which things also we speak," and those who said: "Was not our heart burning within us, when he opened the scriptures to us on the way?" — when, "beginning from the law of Moses down to the prophets, he read to them all things, and revealed the things that were written concerning himself"? Yet a marvelous figure of speech is shown in these things which are written, when it says: "There was not a word out of all that Moses commanded which Jesus did not read in the ears of the whole assembly of Israel." And first, let us see what "he read in the ears" indicates.
